plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the two rotation operations on a binary search tree as a pair of small subtree drawings joined by dotted arrows. On the right, the upper node is a gray circle labeled x with a short stub edge rising to an unnamed parent; x's left edge ends at the Greek letter alpha, and its right edge descends to a second gray circle labeled y whose two edges end at beta and gamma. On the left stands the other configuration: y is now the upper node holding the parent stub, x is y's left child, and the edges terminate at alpha and beta below x and at gamma below y. Subtrees appear only as these labeled edges, without triangles. Between the drawings, an upper dotted arrow points leftward with "LEFT-ROTATE(T, x)" set above it, and a lower dotted arrow points rightward with "RIGHT-ROTATE(T, y)" set beneath it. Placing the before and after shapes side by side isolates what a rotation touches, the link joining x and y and which of them owns the middle subtree beta. The left-to-right order alpha, x, beta, y, gamma survives in both pictures, which is what makes the operation a legal local repair to the pointer structure.

interactionPlan.concept: A tree rotation changes the local vertical depths of nodes by reassigning a few pointers, but strictly preserves the left-to-right inorder sequence of the entire binary search tree.
elements: Left subtree configuration: gray node y (root), gray node x (left child)
Left configuration edges: vertical parent stub rising from y, y's left edge to x, y's right edge to label γ, x's left edge to label α, x's right edge to label β
Right subtree configuration: gray node x (root), gray node y (right child)
Right configuration edges: vertical parent stub rising from x, x's left edge to label α, x's right edge to y, y's left edge to label β, y's right edge to label γ
Transition arrows: dotted left-pointing arrow with label 'LEFT-ROTATE(T, x)' above it
Transition arrows: dotted right-pointing arrow with label 'RIGHT-ROTATE(T, y)' below it
Inorder projection lines: optional vertical dashed guides dropping from each node/label down to a horizontal axis (α, x, β, y, γ)

api.does: Updates node's left pointer and visually moves its left edge to point to child
Updates node's right pointer and visually moves its right edge to point to child
Moves the top-level incoming parent stub so it points to the new root node

interactions.frame: The left subtree immediately redraws its edges to reflect the new assignment. The changed edge flashes red, and nodes shift smoothly to prevent overlap.

input.label: Initial tree
input.default: Left configuration (y as root, x as left child)

interactions.success_check: The structure of the manipulated left tree exactly matches the target right tree.
interactions.teaches: Rotation is a local, constant-time operation that requires exactly three edge updates: moving the 'middle' subtree (beta), reversing the parent-child link between x and y, and updating the incoming link from the rest of the tree.

interactions.label: Show inorder sequence
interactions.teaches: Despite the vertical restructuring, the horizontal left-to-right order (α < x < β < y < γ) is strictly maintained before, during, and after the rotation.

demo_steps.title: Before Rotation
demo_steps.narration: Observe the left configuration. Node y is the root, and x is its left child. The rotation will elevate x and lower y.

demo_steps.title: The Inorder Invariant
demo_steps.narration: Toggle on the inorder guides. Notice that from left to right, the elements strictly follow the order α, x, β, y, γ. A valid rotation never breaks this sequence.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Tree rotations rearrange parent-child pointers to adjust node depths, but visually and structurally, they merely slide nodes up and down along fixed vertical tracks to preserve the binary search property.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw two side-by-side subtree configurations. Nodes x and y are solid gray circles with italic black text. Subtrees α, β, γ are just text labels placed at the ends of the solid edge lines (no triangles around them). The incoming parent link is a short vertical line extending upward from the root of each configuration. Place the dotted left/right arrows horizontally between the two trees. When 'inorderGuides' is Visible, draw faint vertical dashed lines dropping from the center of α, x, β, y, and γ to show they share the exact same horizontal sequence in both the left and right configurations.

authoredContext: The search-tree operations TREE-INSERT and TREE-DELETE, when run on a redblack tree with n keys, take O.lg n/ time. Because they modify the tree, the result may violate the red-black properties enumerated in Section 13.1. To restore these properties, we must change the colors of some of the nodes in the tree and also change the pointer structure. We change the pointer structure through rotation, which is a local operation in a search tree that preserves the binary-search-tree property. Figure 13.2 shows the two kinds of rotations: left rotations and right rotations. When we do a left rotation on a node x, we assume that its right child y is not T:nil; x may be any node in the tree whose right child is not T:nil. The left rotation “pivots” around the link from x to y. It makes y the new root of the subtree, with x as y’s left child and y’s left child as x’s right child.
